cultivar: Lü Xue Ya old tree (traditionally linked to Fuding Dabai)
processing: Today's handling is not separately documented. The name's old sense predates modern recipes, and white tea from this area is typically withered and dried without rolling.
harvest_season: Not documented for the name itself. White tea buds around Fuding are typically picked in early spring.
appearance_dry: Described in old writing only by its fine colour and aroma; Fuding white buds are typically downy and silvery.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold is typical of Fuding bud-rich whites.
appearance_wet: Soft pale buds and leaf are typical of Fuding whites.
taste_profile: Old writing praises only its colour and fragrance, without tasting detail. Fuding bud whites are typically sweet and softly floral.

brewing.notes: Settings typical of a Fuding bud white, to be used for any tea sold under this name.

vintage_note: There is no documented regular market for it as a defined grade. A tea sold under this name is best treated like other Fuding whites, by harvest year, fresh or stored, and you should ask what the seller means by it.
description:
Lü Xue Ya, Green Snow Bud, is one of the oldest names tied to Fuding white tea: both a historical tea of Taimu Shan and an old tree by Hongxue Cave. It matters more as a piece of history than as something you can reliably buy.

The old writing does not give a recipe. It praises colour and fragrance and rates the Hongxue Cave tea best. White tea from the area today is withered and dried without rolling, but that cannot simply be read back onto the historic tea.

Tasting notes for a tea under this name are not documented in any useful way. Expect a Fuding white in the general sweet and softly floral style, and judge the actual lot.

If you see the name for sale, ask whether it is a place, a cultivar or just a poetic label. For learning what Fuding can do, a named silver needle with a clear year is a more certain place to start.
history:
The name appears in Zhou Lianggong's Qing work Min Xiao Ji, in his Min tea songs, and the Republic-era gazetteer of Taimu Shan repeats that Lü Xue Ya is now called bai hao, with the Hongxue Cave tea the finest.

By local legend the old tree at the cave was planted by Taimu herself, and another legend has Chen Huan of Bailiu told in a dream to grow it. Records date his moving plants home to 1857, though some tellings set it in the Guangxu years. A tree at the cave is still shown as this mother plant, and that identification rests on local tradition.
